items.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995
items.q: I think Miles Davis started this years ago

ctx.x: You know I met a lot of fans over in Paris recently, playing for dancing. There’s a couple of little dance clubs that I frequent when I’m over there. And you know you hit it right on the head. They know the tempos that they can do their steps to. So why should musicians say well hey, I want to play this song just a little bit brighter to put an edge on the groove for excitement. Why not slow the tempo down where people can really get in the groove of the music and once you flood the dance floor, you have their…

know, and I look at it that I want to see what you’re made of rhythmically. I want to see how you react to the groove a little bit. So I can play the tempo real slow and juicy and get a groove going, and I know that you will not be able to sit still. You have to get up and start moving, even if there’s no dance floor. You know so that mindset is very important when you’re trying to communicate what is considered contemporary music to the younger people today, because they don’t know about Gene Ammons and Sonny…
One of my favorites of all time was Cannonball Adderley, not only because of the great way that he played but the fact that he talked to the audience—
